captions.cover.b2: In 2023, 130 countries and areas had too few children to replace their parents.
captions.cover.b3: Yet 84 are still growing. | 66 have more births than deaths; 18 grow only because more people arrive than leave.
captions.s1.b0: Three questions. | One: how do births, deaths and migration relate, and differ by region, country and income? | Two: does one indicator tell the whole story, or only several together? | Three: do countries share one road at different speeds, and what should the UN watch?
captions.s1.b1: Population change is bookkeeping: | births minus deaths, plus net migration, arrivals minus departures.
captions.s1.b2: In today's high-income countries, net migration accounted for | about seven in ten of the growth since 2000. | Elsewhere, growth came almost entirely from births exceeding deaths.
captions.s1.b3: Blue: more births than deaths, and growing,
captions.s1.b3b: including 22 below replacement that grow with no net arrivals.
captions.s1.b4a: Light blue: deaths exceed births, but arrivals keep it growing.
captions.s1.b4b: Orange: deaths exceed births, and it shrinks.
captions.s1.b4c: Purple: births exceed deaths, but net departures make it shrink.
captions.s1.b5a: Migration is also the least certain lever.
captions.s1.b5b: For the Emirates in 2050, the UN's 95 percent range is nine to thirty-three million.
captions.s2.b1: Set each country's clock to when its fertility fell below four children, | and the curves line up. | The road is shared; the speed is not. | China went from five to three children in 5 years; Egypt took 33.
captions.s2.b2: Child deaths started falling first in 106 of 109 high-fertility countries. | The gap was typically at least 22 years.
captions.s2.b3: Within one country, this link is smaller than what comparing countries suggests. | A sequence in time, not proof of cause.
captions.s2.b4: Question one, answered: child deaths fell first and births followed, | at each country's pace; latest in low-income countries. | Migration moves on its own, alike among neighbours only in the Gulf, | and weighs most in high-income countries.
captions.s3.b1: Question two. | Fertility alone captures the slow story: | about three quarters of the differences in how old populations are. | Only part of today's growth, and almost none of migration.
captions.s3.b2: Fertility alone finds only one in eight of each country's closest look-alikes.
captions.s3.b3: Countries differ in two separate ways. | Fertility tracks the first, the transition to fewer births and deaths, | but misses migration.
captions.s3.b4: Blend indicators into one score: | the weights can shift one country in five by more than twenty places. | Question two, answered: no. | The Emirates and Belarus share the same fertility; | one grows almost four percent a year, the other shrinks. | The story emerges only when transition and migration are read together.
captions.s4.b1: Question three. | Grouped by seventy-year paths, countries form three stretches of one road, | plus a migration-led group, mostly Gulf states. | Early movers are projected to grow only through migration, or shrink. | Fast movers, India, China and Indonesia, | are projected to age from 30 to 40 in about 32 years. | About as fast as Early movers did, or faster. | Recent movers have the highest child mortality today.
captions.s4.b2: Countries grew closer in life expectancy, but further apart in age.
captions.s4.b3: Question three, answered: mostly one road, at different speeds. | For the UN: watch child survival where it is off pace for the 2030 goal. | Watch ageing where fertility is low but populations still grow. | Watch migration data where growth depends on arrivals.
captions.s4.b4: Projections are labelled as scenarios; examples follow a rule; | hypotheses were fixed before the final run. | These are patterns, not causes; | every number and our AI use are documented in our notebook.
captions.s4.b5: One number can't tell eight billion stories. | But births, deaths and migration, read together region by region, | can tell the UN where to look next.
